body.author: Editorial sample
body.digest: An illustrative four-step routine for collecting, selecting, drafting and reviewing knowledge.
body.content:
A Reviewable Weekly Knowledge Routine

The Question to Ask Each Week

How do you turn scattered reading into output you can actually check? The supplied editorial notes propose a simple answer: split the weekly work into four distinct stages — collection, selection, synthesis, and review — so nothing is published on vibes alone [source:notes].

The Four Steps

  • Collect. Gather material freely, without committing to publish any of it. This keeps exploration cheap [source:notes].
  • Select. Narrow the week's material down to one reader question worth answering [source:notes].
  • Synthesize. Write down the claim and the source that supports it, together, so the two never drift apart [source:notes].
  • Review. Before publishing, check whether the claim, the link, and the illustration actually agree with each other [source:notes].

Why Review Is the Load-Bearing Step

The first three steps produce material; only review makes it trustworthy. Each claim should trace back to a named source, and each illustration should show what the text says it shows.

Hypothetical example: suppose your synthesis step produced the sentence "weekly review improves retention." The review step would flag it, because no source in this routine supports that claim — so it gets cut or rewritten with evidence.

What This Sample Is — and Isn't

This article is a synthetic acceptance fixture, not a research report [source:notes]. It deliberately contains no real statistics, no customer information, and no quotations [source:notes]. The illustration above is a schematic of four stages, not evidence of any measured result [source:notes].

The single source here is a short set of editorial notes — a summary-style document, not a full-text study, and it is not treated as one. The routine itself is the takeaway: collect, select, synthesize, then review before you hit publish [source:notes].
